data.name: About_Installed
data.value: Installed with the installer. Tiresias updates itself from its GitHub releases and asks before restarting.

data.name: About_Development
data.value: A development build: run from a build folder, not installed, so it doesn't update itself. Its tray icon has an orange corner, so you can tell it from the installed app.

data.name: About_NoNotes
data.value: There are no notes for this version in the changelog.

data.name: Consent_Environment_Note
data.value: They go into this one program's environment, and whatever it starts. Allowing it hands over the values; they are never shown here.

data.name: Consent_NuGet_Heading
data.value: Give a NuGet feed's token to {0}?

data.name: Consent_NuGet_Note
data.value: The program uses it to download packages from this feed. Allowing it hands over the value; it is never shown here.

data.name: Consent_Shell_Heading
data.value: Give sealed variables to this {0} terminal?

data.name: Consent_Shell_Note
data.value: This terminal, and everything run from it, keeps them until it closes or Tiresias locks. You're asked again only for names a folder adds.

data.name: Env_AddInvalid
data.value: Type a name (without =) and a value.

data.name: Env_Body
data.value: Variables in your Windows environment are readable by every program you run. Sealed ones are given only to a program you allow: run it with tir run -- <command>.

data.name: Env_FolderInvalid
data.value: The folder must be a full path, such as C:\src\shop.

data.name: Env_FolderPick
data.value: Folder whose commands get this variable

data.name: Env_Locked
data.value: Tiresias is locked. Unlock it with Windows Hello to see or change sealed variables.

data.name: Env_NewFolderHint
data.value: Leave the folder empty for every terminal and tir run. With a folder, the variable is only for commands run in it and below, and overrides one of the same name.

data.name: Env_NothingPicked
data.value: Tick at least one variable first.

data.name: Env_NuGetFoundSummary
data.value: NuGet.Config still gives these feeds their token itself. Move them over: the token is sealed, and NuGet asks Tiresias for it instead.

data.name: Env_NuGetImportBody
data.value: Seals the tokens for {0} and takes their credentials out of {1}. NuGet then asks Tiresias, and you allow each program once.

data.name: Env_NuGetImported
data.value: Moved {0} to Tiresias. NuGet asks for the token from now on.

data.name: Env_NuGetNone
data.value: No NuGet.Config in your profile has credentials for a feed, and no feed uses a sealed variable.

data.name: Env_NuGetProtect
data.value: %{0}% in {1}: seals {0}, now in your Windows environment

data.name: Env_NuGetRemoved
data.value: NuGet no longer gets a sealed variable for {0}. The variables stay sealed.

data.name: Env_NuGetSealClearText
data.value: token in plain text in {1}: seals it as {0}

data.name: Env_NuGetSummary
data.value: NuGet asks Tiresias for {0} feed(s), and you allow each program once. Needs the .NET 9.0.200 SDK or later.

data.name: Env_PlaceholderAdded
data.value: Handed out as a placeholder from now on: {0}. Terminals pick it up at their next folder change.

data.name: Env_PlaceholderBaseUrlHint
data.value: The variable the tool reads its API address from. Left empty, it follows the key's name: OPENAI_API_KEY gives OPENAI_BASE_URL.

data.name: Env_PlaceholderBaseUrlSealed
data.value: {0} is itself a sealed variable, so it can't also carry the forwarder's address.

data.name: Env_PlaceholderNeedsBaseUrl
data.value: Name the variable the tool reads its API address from (for example OPENAI_BASE_URL).

data.name: Env_PlaceholderNoServices
data.value: No https service in the vault for a placeholder to stand in for. Add one under Services, with the key as its secret ("Bearer <key>").

data.name: Env_PlaceholderPickOne
data.value: Check one variable in the global set to hand out as a placeholder.

data.name: Env_PlaceholderRemoved
data.value: Handed out as the value again: {0}.

data.name: Env_PlaceholderSummary
data.value: Check one sealed API key above, pick the vault service whose secret is that key ("Bearer <key>"), and Tiresias hands out a tirph_ placeholder with the forwarder's address instead of the key.

data.name: Env_Protected

data.name: Env_PutBackDone
data.value: Put {0} back in Windows. Programs started from now on can read them again.

data.name: Env_PutBackFolder
data.value: A folder's variables never came from Windows, so there is nothing to put back. Remove them instead.

data.name: Env_RemoveBody
data.value: {0} will be deleted, not put back in Windows. Only do this if you no longer need the values.

data.name: Env_SealedSummary
data.value: {0} sealed. Tick some to put them back in Windows or remove them.

data.name: Env_WindowsSummary
data.value: {0} look like secrets and are ticked. Sealing removes them from Windows once the sealed copy reads back; programs already running keep their copy until they restart.

data.name: Environment_Locked

data.name: Environment_NoneSealed

data.name: Environment_NotSealed

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryRestore_Body
data.value: This PC already has sealed secrets: copied from another PC, or left by an earlier setup. Windows Hello here can't open them, but the recovery key they were sealed with can. Type it from your paper copy and they open on this PC as before; this PC then uses the same recovery key, so the paper you have keeps covering everything. Spaces and case don't matter.

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryRestore_KeyName
data.value: Recovery key the secrets were sealed with

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryRestore_Later
data.value: Continue to finish setup. When you find the key those were sealed with, use Restore on the status page.

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryRestore_LostBody
data.value: You can create a new recovery key and carry on. Secrets you seal from now on are covered by it, but the ones already here stay locked until their own key turns up; the status page offers to restore them whenever it does.

data.name: NuGet_BadSource
data.value: NuGet asked for a source that isn't a URL.

data.name: NuGet_Refused
data.value: the feed refused {0} for {1}. Check the token, then seal the new one with tir env set {0}.

data.name: NuGet_VariableMissing
data.value: {1} is mapped to {0}, which is no longer sealed. Seal it again with tir env set {0}.

data.name: Recovery_Body
data.value: Some sealed secrets on this PC don't open with its Windows Hello: they were copied from another PC, or Windows Hello was reset since they were sealed. Type the recovery key they were sealed with. Nothing is decrypted or re-encrypted: each secret gets a copy of its key for this PC's Windows Hello, and keeps its recovery copy. Spaces and case don't matter.

data.name: Recovery_KeyAdopted
data.value: This PC now uses this recovery key for new secrets too.

data.name: Recovery_NotOpened
data.value: Still locked, sealed with another recovery key: {0}. Restore again with that key.

data.name: Recovery_OtherKeyKept
data.value: This PC keeps its own recovery key as well, because secrets sealed here since setup need it. Keep both papers.

data.name: Recovery_Services
data.value: Services already running pick up restored vault secrets the next time you unlock.

data.name: Secrets_FolderPickTitle
data.value: Folder to look for projects in

data.name: Secrets_NoFolders
data.value: Add the folder you keep your code in, and projects show by name instead of by id. Only project files are read.

data.name: Secrets_NoProjectDetail
data.value: No project in the scanned folders uses this id. It may be left over from a copied folder, or its project lives somewhere not scanned.

data.name: Secrets_NotScannedDetail
data.value: No project is linked to this id yet. Add the folder you keep your code in under Project folders, or use Find a project.

data.name: Secrets_RecycleBody
data.value: No project in {1} uses the user secrets you picked ({0} folder(s)). A project kept somewhere else still could. They go to the Recycle Bin, so you can put them back from there.

data.name: Secrets_RecycleFailed
data.value: Couldn't move {0} to the Recycle Bin; a program may have it open. Close it and try again.

data.name: Secrets_Scanned
data.value: {0} of {1} named after their project. Rescanned each time this window opens.

data.name: Shell_NotUnlocked
data.value: not unlocked ({0}), so this terminal has no sealed variables. Run Update-TiresiasEnvironment -Ask to try again.

data.name: Shell_Refused
data.value: not given to this terminal. Run Update-TiresiasEnvironment -Ask to be asked again.

data.name: Shell_Unrecognised
data.value: couldn't tell which terminal asked, so nothing was given. Check that the hook passes $PID (tir env hook).

data.name: Status_RestoreBody
data.value: Sealed items that don't open with this PC's Windows Hello: {0}. They came from another PC, or Windows Hello was reset. The recovery key they were sealed with gives them back.

data.name: Status_RestoreTitle
data.value: Some secrets need your recovery key

data.name: Status_ReviewEnvironment
data.value: Seal environment variables that look like secrets

data.name: Status_StartWithWindows
data.value: Start Tiresias when I sign in to Windows

data.name: Status_StartWithWindowsDev
data.value: Only an installed copy can start at sign-in; a development build's folder changes with every build.

data.name: Status_StartWithWindowsFailed
data.value: Couldn't change the sign-in setting. The app log has the details.

data.name: Status_StartWithWindowsNote
data.value: Apps that start at sign-in and use protected user secrets wait up to a minute for it.

data.name: Startup_SwitchHeading
data.value: Another copy of Tiresias is running

data.name: Startup_SwitchBody
data.value:
Tiresias {0} is running from {1}.
Switch to this copy, {2}, from {3}? The other copy quits first, ending its lease, and this one starts locked.

data.name: Startup_SwitchBusy
data.value: The running copy is waiting on an open window: a consent question, the secrets editor, services or setup. Finish or close it, then start this copy again.

data.name: Startup_SwitchOld
data.value: The copy that is running is older and can't hand over. Quit it from its tray menu, then start this copy again.

data.name: Startup_SwitchFailed
data.value: The other copy didn't quit within 15 seconds. Quit it from its tray menu, then start this copy again.

data.name: Startup_AlreadyRunning
data.value: Tiresias is already running. Look for its icon in the notification area, next to the clock (it may be behind the ^ arrow).

data.name: Startup_OtherAgent
data.value: Another Tiresias agent is running in this session, probably 'tir agent' in a terminal. Only one can serve your secrets at a time. Stop it (press q in that terminal), then start Tiresias again.

data.name: Tray_UnlockedNoLease
data.value: Unlocked, no lease: unlock again to retry

data.name: Tray_ModeSolo
data.value: Solo: the broker runs in this app

data.name: Tray_UpdateReady
data.value: Update to {0} available - restart to apply

data.name: Unlock_NoLease
data.value: Unlocked for user secrets, but the lease didn't open: {0}

data.name: Control_NewerTir
data.value: This tir is newer than the Tiresias app. Update the app, then try again.

data.name: Control_Unknown
data.value: The Tiresias app doesn't know the request '{0}'. Update the app, then try again.

data.name: Consent_UserSecrets_Heading
data.value: An app wants the user secrets of {0}

data.name: Consent_UserSecrets_KeysLabel
data.value: It will get these {0} keys (values stay hidden here):

data.name: Consent_UserSecrets_KeysLabelOne
data.value: It will get this key (its value stays hidden here):

data.name: Consent_UserSecrets_Note
data.value: Allow for this session lasts until you lock Tiresias or for 12 hours, whichever comes first.

data.name: Consent_Placeholder_Heading
data.comment: {0}: what tir is asking for, e.g. tir exec gh

data.name: Consent_Placeholder_Note
data.value: After you allow it, tir asks for Windows Hello to confirm it's you.

data.name: Consent_Countdown
data.value: If you don't answer, this is denied in {0}.

data.name: Consent_Unlock_Label
data.value: Tiresias is locked, so its secrets can't be opened yet.

data.name: Consent_Unlock_Note
data.value: Unlock to answer: you then see which keys it gets and choose whether to allow it. Deny, and the app stops at startup.

data.name: Consent_NotMe_Tip
data.value: You didn't expect this request: deny it, lock Tiresias and block this program.

data.name: Lockdown_UnlockFromApp
data.value: Tiresias is locked because you chose "This wasn't me". Unlock it from the Tiresias tray icon or status page.

data.name: Incident_What
data.value: You said you didn't expect: {0}. Tiresias denied it, locked, ended its lease and forgot every "Allow for this session", including terminals and NuGet.

data.name: Incident_Blocked
data.value: Blocked: Tiresias refuses this program without asking, even after you unlock, until you unblock it on the status page.

data.name: Incident_NotBlocked
data.value: Tiresias couldn't tell which file this program is, so it isn't blocked. Everything is refused until you unlock.

data.name: Incident_ParentsUnknown
data.value: Unknown: the process has ended, or Windows didn't say.

data.name: Incident_ProcessNotFound
data.value: Tiresias couldn't find this program running.

data.name: Incident_ScanBody
data.value: In Windows Security, open Virus & threat protection, then Scan options, choose Custom scan and pick the folder above. A Full scan checks everything.

data.name: Incident_Unlock
data.value: Every request is refused until you unlock with Windows Hello from the Tiresias tray icon or status page. Nothing else on this PC was changed.

data.name: Status_LockedDown
data.value: Locked after "This wasn't me": every request is refused until you unlock here.

data.name: Problem_Copied
data.value: Details copied. Paste them into a support request or issue.

data.name: Problem_HelloNotSetUp_What
data.value: This Windows account has no PIN, face or fingerprint sign-in.

data.name: Problem_HelloNotSetUp_Why
data.value: Tiresias unlocks your secrets with Windows Hello, so only you, at this PC, can open them.

data.name: Problem_HelloNotSetUp_Next
data.value: Set up a PIN (or face or fingerprint) in Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options, then try again.

data.name: Problem_HelloCancelled_What
data.value: The Windows Hello prompt was closed before it finished.

data.name: Problem_HelloCancelled_Why
data.value: Tiresias stays locked, so apps asking for secrets are told to wait until you unlock.

data.name: Problem_HelloCancelled_Next
data.value: Try again when you're ready. Nothing was changed.

data.name: Problem_HelloExpired_What
data.value: The prompt was answered too late. This happens when it waits for minutes behind other windows.

data.name: Problem_HelloExpired_Why
data.value: Tiresias stays locked, so apps asking for secrets are told to wait until you unlock.

data.name: Problem_HelloExpired_Next
data.value: Try again and answer the prompt when it appears. A prompt Windows keeps behind other windows flashes in the taskbar.

data.name: Problem_HelloCredentialMissing_Title
data.value: The Windows Hello key for Tiresias is gone

data.name: Problem_HelloCredentialMissing_What
data.value: Windows no longer has the Hello key Tiresias created. This happens after a Hello reset or on a new PC.

data.name: Problem_HelloCredentialMissing_Why
data.value: Secrets sealed to the old key can't be opened with Hello any more. Your paper recovery key still opens them.

data.name: Problem_HelloCredentialMissing_Next
data.value: Finish setup again to create a new Windows Hello key. The status page then offers Restore: type your paper recovery key and your sealed secrets open with the new key.

data.name: Problem_HelloUnavailable_What
data.value: Windows reported a problem with Hello, for example the security chip is busy or locked after too many attempts.

data.name: Problem_HelloUnavailable_Why
data.value: Tiresias stays locked until Hello works.

data.name: Problem_HelloUnavailable_Next
data.value: Wait a moment and try again. If it keeps failing, sign out of Windows and back in.

data.name: Problem_BrokerUnreachable_What
data.value: Tiresias couldn't reach the broker that holds your leased secrets.

data.name: Problem_BrokerUnreachable_Why
data.value: Placeholders and tir exec need the broker. User secrets still work.

data.name: Problem_BrokerUnreachable_Next
data.value: Check your network or VPN connection, then try again. The status page shows which check fails.

data.name: Problem_BrokerRefused_Title
data.value: Unlocked, but the lease didn't open

data.name: Problem_BrokerRefused_What
data.value: Windows Hello worked, but the broker declined to open today's lease.

data.name: Problem_BrokerRefused_Why
data.value: User secrets work. Placeholders and tir exec need the lease.

data.name: Problem_BrokerRefused_Next
data.value: The details say why. The status page checks the trust chain and the broker.

data.name: Problem_SoloBrokerDown_What
data.value: In solo mode the broker runs inside this app, and it couldn't start.

data.name: Problem_SoloBrokerDown_Why
data.value: Placeholders and tir exec need it. User secrets still work.

data.name: Problem_SoloBrokerDown_Next
data.value: If another program uses port 7780, close it and try again. The details say what went wrong.

data.name: Problem_VaultUnreadable_Title
data.value: A Tiresias file can't be read

data.name: Problem_VaultUnreadable_What
data.value: A vault or secrets file is damaged or in a format this version doesn't know.

data.name: Problem_VaultUnreadable_Why
data.value: Tiresias won't guess at its contents, so the secrets in it can't be used until it's fixed.

data.name: Problem_VaultUnreadable_Next
data.value: Restore the file from a backup, or update Tiresias if a newer version wrote it. The data folder holds the vault.

data.name: Problem_NoRecoveryKey_What
data.value: Tiresias won't seal secrets until a paper recovery key exists.

data.name: Problem_NoRecoveryKey_Why
data.value: Without one, losing Windows Hello or this PC would lose the secrets for good.

data.name: Problem_NoRecoveryKey_Next
data.value: Finish setup to create the recovery key. It takes a minute and a pen.

data.name: Problem_FileAccess_Title
data.value: A file couldn't be read or written

data.name: Problem_FileAccess_What
data.value: Windows refused access to a Tiresias file, or the disk is full.

data.name: Problem_FileAccess_Why
data.value: The change you made wasn't saved.

data.name: Problem_FileAccess_Next
data.value: Check the data folder's permissions and free space, then try again.

data.name: Problem_Unexpected_What
data.value: Tiresias hit a problem it has no better explanation for.

data.name: Problem_Unexpected_Why
data.value: Your secrets are still sealed; nothing was written in clear.

data.name: Problem_Unexpected_Next
data.value: Try again. If it happens again, copy the details and open an issue on the Tiresias repository.

data.name: Status_ModeSolo
data.value: Solo mode: the broker runs inside this app on this PC.

data.name: Status_ModeNone
data.value: No solo broker on this PC.

data.value: {0} is now sealed. From its next start, Tiresias asks you before it gets them.

data.name: Secrets_SealConfirmBody
data.value:
The secrets of {0} will be encrypted on disk. From then on, only apps that use Tiresias.Extensions.Configuration can read them, and only after you allow it.
An app that doesn't use it yet starts without these secrets. You can undo this here with Store in clear.
Seal them now?

data.name: Secrets_ClearConfirmTitle
data.value: Store these user secrets in clear?

data.name: Secrets_ClearConfirmBody
data.value:
The secrets of {0} will be written back as a plain secrets.json. Any program running as you can read them again, and Tiresias no longer asks before an app gets them.
Use this for an app that can't use Tiresias.Extensions.Configuration.
Store them in clear?

data.value: Stored in clear. Seal now encrypts them again.

data.name: Secrets_StatePick
data.value: Pick a project to see its keys.

data.name: Secrets_StateNoProjects
data.value: No project on this PC has user secrets yet. Use Find a project to start with one.

data.name: Secrets_StateLocked
data.value: Tiresias is locked. Unlock to see and edit this project's secrets.

data.name: Secrets_StateNotSealed
data.value: {0}, still in clear on disk. Saving seals them.

data.name: Secrets_StateUnreadable
data.value: This project's secrets file can't be opened.

data.name: Secrets_LockedCannotSave
data.value: Unlock first: saving seals the file with your Windows Hello key.

data.name: Secrets_UnsavedBody
data.value: You have changes that aren't saved. Save them before closing?

data.name: FirstRun_Welcome_Body
data.value: Tiresias keeps your API keys and app secrets encrypted on this PC and lets tools and AI agents use them without seeing them. You approve each use, and every decision is logged.

data.name: FirstRun_Welcome_Steps
data.value: Setup takes about two minutes: you confirm with Windows Hello, write down a recovery key on paper, and pick how you want to run Tiresias. You can close this window and continue later.

data.name: FirstRun_Hello_Body
data.value: Tiresias creates its own Windows Hello key, kept in this PC's security chip. Your secrets open only after your PIN, face or fingerprint.

data.name: FirstRun_Hello_Note
data.value: Windows asks you to confirm in its own dialog.

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryShow_Body
data.value: If you lose Windows Hello or this PC, this key is the only way back into your secrets. Write it on paper and keep it somewhere safe.

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryShow_Warning
data.value: It is shown only now and is not stored anywhere. Don't save it in a file or take a screenshot (this window can't be captured anyway).

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryShow_Confirm
data.value: I wrote it down on paper

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryShow_NotConfirmed
data.value: Tick the box once the key is on paper.

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryConfirm_Body
data.value: Type two groups from the key you wrote down. Groups are counted from 1, left to right.

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryConfirm_Mismatch
data.value: Those groups don't match. Check what you wrote and try again, or show the key again.

data.name: FirstRun_Mode_Title
data.value: How do you want to run Tiresias?

data.name: FirstRun_Mode_SoloBody
data.value: Everything runs on this PC; no server needed. Trade-off: requests leave from your own connection, and the secrets stay on the same machine as your tools.

data.name: FirstRun_Mode_BrokerBody
data.value: Your team or your own server runs the broker. You enrol this PC with tir enroll, using the details from whoever runs it.

data.name: FirstRun_Mode_SecretsOnly
data.value: Just protect user secrets for now

data.name: FirstRun_Mode_SecretsOnlyBody
data.value: Seal your .NET user secrets. Placeholders and tir exec need solo mode or a broker; you can set that up later.

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryType_Body
data.value: Setup was interrupted after your recovery key was shown. Solo mode signs this PC's trust chain with it, so type it from your paper copy. Spaces and case don't matter.

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryType_Invalid
data.value: That isn't a recovery key. It's groups of letters A-Z and digits 2-7, as written on your paper copy.

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryType_Lost
data.value: I don't have my recovery key

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryType_LostCanReplace
data.value: Nothing is sealed to it yet, so you can make a new one and write that down instead.

data.name: FirstRun_RecoveryType_LostKeep
data.value: Some secrets are already sealed to that key, so it can't be replaced here: it is their only way back if Hello is lost. You can keep using Tiresias for user secrets and set up solo mode once you find it.

data.name: FirstRun_Done_Solo
data.value: Tiresias runs in solo mode: the broker is part of this app, and it is unlocked now.

data.name: FirstRun_Done_Broker
data.value: To use your broker, run tir enroll with the details from whoever runs it. Until then, Tiresias protects your user secrets.

data.name: FirstRun_Done_SecretsOnly
data.value: Tiresias protects your .NET user secrets. Set up solo mode or a broker any time from the tray menu.

data.name: FirstRun_Done_Tray
data.value: Tiresias lives in the notification area, next to the clock. Use its menu to unlock, lock, edit secrets and see activity.

data.name: FirstRun_Done_Next
data.value: Next: add the Tiresias.Extensions.Configuration package to a project and start it. Its secrets are sealed on first run.

data.name: Update_Body
data.value: It is downloaded. Restarting takes a few seconds: Tiresias locks, updates and starts again, and you unlock once more. If the update can't be applied, the current version keeps running.

data.name: Update_Busy
data.value: Finish what's open first (an approval, the secrets editor, the Services page or setup), then choose the update in the tray menu again.

data.name: Services_StateUnlocked
data.value: These are the services tir exec can reach through the broker. Adding one takes effect at its next request; you don't need to lock and unlock.

data.name: Services_StateLocked
data.value: Tiresias is locked. You can see and remove services; unlock to add one with a new secret.

data.name: Services_GrantSecretMissing
data.value: , secret missing from the vault: add the service again to type it

data.name: Services_None
data.value: No services yet. Choose Add to set one up.

data.name: Services_Unreadable
data.value: The vault file can't be read. Open the data folder from the status page and check vault.json.

data.name: Policy_Body
data.value:
Tiresias uses your secrets only as you approve here, so a program that edits the vault file can't send them elsewhere. Windows Hello asks next.
{0}

data.name: Policy_MigrateBody
data.value:
Tiresias will now refuse changes to these settings unless you approve them, so a program that edits the vault file can't send your secrets elsewhere. Until you approve, these services don't work. Windows Hello asks next.
{0}

data.name: Policy_Declined
data.value: Not saved: you didn't approve the change.

data.name: Services_RemoveConfirmBody
data.value: Remove {0}? Programs can no longer reach it through Tiresias. Its secret stays in the vault, so you can add the service again without typing it. Windows Hello asks next.

data.name: Services_Removed
data.value: Removed {0}. Its secret is still in the vault.

data.name: Services_SlugHint
data.value: Used in tir exec <name>. Lower-case letters, digits and dashes, like httpbin.

data.name: Services_UpstreamHint
data.value: Where requests go, starting with https://, like https://api.example.com.

data.name: Services_SecretHint
data.value: Pick a secret already in the vault, or leave empty to create one named after the service.

data.name: Services_SecretExists
data.value: Uses {0}, already in the vault. Nothing to type.

data.name: Services_SecretNew
data.value: {0} isn't in the vault yet: type its value below.

data.name: Services_ValueHint
data.value: The whole Authorization header, like Bearer sk-.... It is sealed with Windows Hello and never shown again.

data.name: Services_ValueEmpty
data.value: Type the secret's value, the whole Authorization header.

data.name: Services_ValueLocked
data.value: Unlock first: a new secret is sealed with Windows Hello.

data.name: Services_MethodsHint
data.value: Separated by commas, like GET, POST. GET when empty.

data.name: Services_AllowHint
data.value: One regular expression per line, matched against path and query.

data.name: Services_AllowEveryPath

data.name: Services_ElevationHint

data.name: Services_Added
data.value: Added {0}. Programs started with tir exec {0} can use it now.

data.name: Services_AddedEveryPath
data.value: Added {0}, with every path allowed. To narrow it, remove it and add it again with allowed paths.

data.name: Services_ProblemSlugInvalid

data.name: Services_SqlSaved
data.value: Saved {0}. Apps reach it with tiresias:sql/{0}/read or /write in their user secrets.

data.name: Sql_WindowTitle
data.value: Set up a SQL Server - Tiresias

data.name: Sql_Intro
data.value: Prepares one database so apps get a temporary login for each lease instead of a password in their user secrets. Logins can read, or read and write; never change the schema. They are dropped when the lease ends.

data.name: Sql_ServerHint
data.value: As SQL Server Management Studio takes it: sql.example.com, sql.example.com,1433 or sql.example.com\SQLEXPRESS.

data.name: Sql_DatabaseHint
data.value: It must exist already. One database per server can be set up.

data.name: Sql_SlugHint
data.value: What apps and tir use to name it. Lower-case letters, digits and dashes.

data.name: Sql_TrustHint
data.value: The connection is always encrypted. Tick this only for a server you know whose certificate this PC doesn't trust, such as a development server on your own network.

data.name: Sql_AdminIntro
data.value: Once, to create the logins and procedures. This sign-in is used by this window only and is not saved anywhere.

data.name: Sql_UserMissing
data.value: Type the login and its password, or use Windows authentication.

data.name: Sql_Locked
data.value: Tiresias is locked. Unlock it, then try again: the connection is sealed to Windows Hello.

data.name: Sql_StepStopped
data.value: Stopped. Nothing was saved to the vault; running the setup again is safe.

data.name: Sql_ProvisionerExistsTitle
data.value: Give the provisioner a new password?

data.name: Sql_ProvisionerExistsBody
data.value: {0} already has a tiresias_provisioner login, perhaps set up from another PC. Setting up gives it a new password, and any other Tiresias vault that uses it stops getting logins until it is set up again from there.

data.name: Sql_DoneBody
data.value: In an app's user secrets (Manage User Secrets in Visual Studio), use this instead of a connection string:

data.name: Sql_DoneWrite
data.value: Use /write instead of /read for an app that saves data. The app needs the Tiresias.Extensions.Configuration package, and gets a new login before the old one expires.

data.name: Services_RavenSaved
data.value: Saved {0}. Apps reach it with tiresias:raven/{0} as their RavenDB URL.

data.name: Raven_Intro
data.value: Keeps a RavenDB client certificate in the vault, so apps connect through Tiresias with a URL in their user secrets instead of a .pfx file on disk. What the app may read or write is the certificate's own access on the server.

data.name: Raven_ServerHint
data.value: The address RavenDB Studio opens on, e.g. https://a.raven.example.com or https://a.raven.example.com:8080. For a cluster, any one node.

data.name: Raven_DatabaseHint
data.value: The database the app uses. Tiresias checks the certificate can reach it before saving.

data.name: Raven_ChangesHint
data.value: For apps that subscribe to changes (store.Changes()). It keeps a connection open for as long as the lease lasts; leave it off unless the app needs it.

data.name: Raven_CertificateIntro
data.value: The .pfx RavenDB gave you for this app, registered on the server. Tiresias checks it, then seals it in the vault; you can delete the file afterwards.

data.name: Raven_NeedsPassword
data.value: The file has a password: type it below.

data.name: Raven_PasswordHint
data.value: Leave it empty if the file has none. It is used to open the file here only; the vault keeps the certificate without it.

data.name: Raven_Locked
data.value: Tiresias is locked. Unlock it, then try again: the certificate is sealed to Windows Hello.

data.name: Raven_StepStopped
data.value: Stopped. Nothing was saved to the vault.

data.name: Raven_DoneBody
data.value: In an app's user secrets (Manage User Secrets in Visual Studio), use this instead of a URL and certificate:

data.name: Raven_DoneCode
data.value: Pass the URL to the DocumentStore as usual and leave its Certificate unset: Tiresias presents the certificate. The app needs the Tiresias.Extensions.Configuration package.

data.name: Raven_EditDatabaseHint
data.value: Tiresias doesn't keep the database name: type the one the app uses, to check the certificate against it and for the user secrets line.

data.name: Raven_Keeps
data.value: The certificate stays as it is in the vault. Pick a file only to replace it.

data.name: Services_Saved
data.value: Saved {0}. Programs using it get the change at once.

data.name: Usage_RavenDatabase
data.value: Replace <database> with the database the app uses.

data.name: Usage_PlaceholderBody
data.value: If the service's secret is an API key sent as Authorization: Bearer, a terminal can get a placeholder for it instead of the key:

data.name: Usage_PlaceholderHint
data.value: Or in the Environment variables window: check the sealed key, pick {0} under Hand out a placeholder instead, then Use a placeholder. Name the variable after the key the tool reads; the base URL variable points the tool at Tiresias.

data.name: Finding_ReasonLabel
data.value: Why? It stays dismissed until it changes.

data.name: Finding_CopyFailed
data.value: The clipboard is busy. Run this yourself: {0}

data.name: Finding_RecycleHeading
data.value: Move the certificate file to the Recycle Bin?

data.name: Finding_RecycleBody
data.value: The certificate is sealed in Tiresias now, and the broker presents it. The copy at {0} can still be read by any program running as you. Programs that read the file need to use tiresias:raven first.

data.name: Finding_RecycleFailed
data.value: {0} couldn't be moved; it may be open in another program.

data.name: Finding_DisableStartupBody
data.value: It stays installed and you can open it whenever you need it. Turn it back on in Settings, Apps, Startup.

data.name: Finding_StartupOff
data.value: {0} no longer starts at log-on. Turn it back on in Settings, Apps, Startup.

data.name: Installed_Intro
data.value: Every program in the installed-apps list, those you haven't opened in 90 days first. Last opened is the last time you started something in its folder from Start, the taskbar or Explorer; Windows doesn't record other use, so that shows as unknown, never as unused.

data.name: Installed_UseBackground
data.value: Unknown: part of it works without being opened (a tray icon, a service, a driver, something that starts at log-on, or a command on PATH), which Windows doesn't record

data.name: Installed_UseNotRecorded
data.value: Unknown: Windows has no record of you opening anything in its folder, or it names no folder of its own

data.name: Installed_UseRecentNoRun
data.value: Not recorded, but it used credentials through Tiresias in the last 90 days

data.name: Finding_RemoveEntryBody
data.value: Tiresias saves the entry to a .reg file first, then removes it from the installed apps list. Nothing on disk is deleted. Open the saved file to put the entry back.

data.name: Finding_EntryRemoved
data.value: Removed the entry for {0}. It is saved in {1}; open that file to put it back.

data.name: Notify_Decoy_Title
data.value: A program used a decoy credential

data.name: Notify_Decoy_Body
data.value: {0} connected with {1}. Tiresias blocked it until you review it on Home.
data.comment: {0}: program file name; {1}: which decoy, e.g. "the decoy admin token"

data.name: Notify_DecoyRead_Title
data.value: A program opened a decoy file

data.name: Notify_DecoyRead_Body
data.value: {0} opened the decoy file {1}. That may be harmless; Tiresias blocked nothing. See Home.
data.comment: {0}: program file name; {1}: decoy file name, e.g. "passwords.txt"

data.name: Notify_Decoy_Unknown
data.value: A program connected with {0}, but it couldn't be named. See Home.

data.name: Finding_RemoveExtensionBody
data.value: Tiresias runs {0}. You can install the extension again from {1} later.

data.name: Finding_RemoveFailed
data.value: {0} couldn't be removed. Run this yourself: {1}

data.name: Needs_Search
data.value: Describe it, or pick one below

data.name: Needs_SearchHint
data.value: For example "OpenAI key for a script" or "my EF Core app talks to Azure SQL". What you type is matched on this PC and never sent anywhere.

data.name: Finding_TokenBody
data.value: Tiresias reads the token in {0} once, seals it as {1}, and takes it out of the file. Programs then get it only through tir run or a terminal with the hook, after you allow them.

data.name: Position_NothingToCopyTip
data.value: The service accepts who you are; there is no secret to copy.

data.name: Position_ShortLivedTip
data.value: Made for this run and useless after it.

data.name: Position_BrokerOnlyTip
data.value: The program gets a stand-in that is useless anywhere else.

data.name: Position_SealedTip
data.value: Encrypted on disk, handed to the program as its value.

data.name: Position_ReadableTip
data.value: Anything running as you can read it.

data.name: Position_ApprovedTip
data.value: Each program needs your OK, and every use is recorded.

data.name: Position_RecordedTip
data.value: Every use is recorded, but nothing asks.

data.name: Position_SilentTip
data.value: Any program running as you can use it, and nothing records it.

data.name: Consent_AllowSession_Says
data.value: It isn't asked again until Tiresias locks.

data.name: Consent_AllowOnce_Says
data.value: This request only: it is asked again next time.

data.name: Consent_Unlock_Says
data.value: Then you see what it gets, and choose.

data.name: Secrets_RecycleEmptyBody
data.value: The user secrets you picked hold no keys ({0} folder(s)). dotnet user-secrets set creates a folder again when a project needs one. They go to the Recycle Bin, so you can put them back from there.

data.name: Secrets_StateSealedEmpty
data.value: Sealed, but empty: there is nothing in it to protect. Move it to the Recycle Bin, or add keys.

data.name: Secrets_NothingToSeal
data.value: Nothing to seal: this file holds no keys.

data.name: Installed_SignedBy
data.value: {0}, a valid signature (checked on this PC)

data.name: Installed_SignedNoName
data.value: A valid signature without a name (checked on this PC)

data.name: Installed_SignedInvalid
data.value: A signature that is not valid; it names {0}, which anyone can write

data.name: Installed_SignerUnknown
data.value: Not checked: a part of Windows or a Store app, or no program file found

data.name: Installed_SearchOnlineTip
data.value: Opens your browser with a web search for this name and version

data.name: Decoys_Intro
data.value: Fake credentials that work nowhere. A program that uses one is named and blocked until you say it was you.

data.name: Decoys_WhereProject
data.value: {0}, a new folder with an appsettings.Production.json and a .env

data.name: Decoys_PlaceBody
data.value: Tiresias creates {0}, holding a fake database password, admin token and API key that work nowhere. Nothing that exists is changed. A program that uses one is named and blocked. Remove decoys takes it away again.

data.name: Decoys_RemoveBody
data.value: Tiresias deletes the files and variables it placed, and a decoy folder when nothing else is in it.

data.name: Decoys_RemoveKept
data.value: Kept {0}: changed since Tiresias placed it, so it is yours now.
